title: The upper-bound conjecture for the Ova-Ova-Prime-Ova construction
statement: Let the preceding Ova-Ova-Prime-Ova construction be given, and let $N$ denote the number of primes it produces. **The Ova-Ova-Prime-Ova counting conjecture.** Although the preceding theorem guarantees at least one resulting prime, one has $N\leq 10$. The source supplies examples and asserts this as a bound, but gives no independent resolution evidence.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04522

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of April 2021).
source_name: Yeisson Alexis Acevedo Agudelo, “Prime numbers. An alternative study using ova-angular rotations”, arXiv:2104.04522 (2021).

progress.label: Open · solution reported
progress.tldr: A posted calculation claims the ten-output limit is false by producing $38$ outputs from one pair of input primes, but nobody has independently verified it.
progress.summary:
The conjecture asserts that the Ova-Ova-Prime-Ova construction produces at most $10$ primes. Yeisson Alexis Acevedo Agudelo introduced the underlying construction in a 2021 preprint, which records an existence result but does not independently settle this upper bound.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04522)*

**Known results**

- Acevedo Agudelo (2021) gives the construction and guarantees at least one resulting prime, while supplying examples supporting the proposed bound $N\le 10$.


**Posted attempt**

A reader supplies two input primes, $677$ and $401$, and lists $38$ residues satisfying the construction’s primality conditions, claiming $N=38$ and thereby refuting both $N\le 10$ and the earlier bound $N\le 13$. The calculation has not been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): The published construction and at-least-one-output result are recorded, while the ten-output conjecture has a specific but unverified claimed counterexample with $N=38$.

*Caveats. The claimed counterexample appears only in unverified reader-written discussion.*

solutions.body:
Take the primes
\[
\rho_1=677=317+360\cdot1,
\qquad
\rho_2=401=41+360\cdot1.
\]
Their residues are \(k_{\rho_1}=317\) and \(k_{\rho_2}=41\), and both rotation frequencies are \(1\). Thus a residue \(r\) contributes an output of the prescribed construction precisely when
\[
\gcd(r,360)=1,\qquad
k_{\rho_1}+k_{\rho_2}+2-r=360-r\ \text{is prime},
\qquad
r+360(1+1)=720+r\ \text{is prime}.
\]

The following \(38\) distinct residues satisfy all three conditions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
r\in\{&
7,13,23,49,53,67,77,89,91,103,109,119,133,137,161,163,167,187,209,\\
&221,233,247,251,257,263,271,277,289,293,299,301,313,319,329,331,341,343,349
\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, the first eleven give
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
r&360-r&720+r\\\hline
7&353&727\\
13&347&733\\
23&337&743\\
49&311&769\\
53&307&773\\
67&293&787\\
77&283&797\\
89&271&809\\
91&269&811\\
103&257&823\\
109&251&829
\end{array}
\]
and every entry in the last two columns is prime.

Consequently this single pair of input primes produces \(N=38\) prime outputs, contradicting the stated bound \(N\le10\). The earlier published version of the construction proposed the weaker bound \(N\le13\); the same example disproves that original bound as well.
